Hand-cranked equipment was replaced by steam-driven machinery whenever volume justified the outlay. With more hired hands on the floor, Hieronymus could no longer keep instructions in his head. Recipes were rewritten for fifty-pound kettles, batch standards were hung on the walls, and mixing rules became mandatory.

Matilda enforced that discipline strictly. She insisted on daily inventory logs, detailed tare weights for raw imports, and formal records of every formula adjustment. If a shipment of cacao arrived with excess debris, she noted the deduction. If Hieronymus altered a batch of nut paste on the fly without telling the office, she brought the book to him before the day was out.

That expanding operation eventually took shape as the Brickhouse Square factory. It was assembled piece by piece over several years - a brick warehouse here, a boiler room addition there, new cooling tables, and a dedicated packing floor. By the late 1860s, Baumeister Confections was operating as a serious industrial manufacturer.

The product lines evolved alongside the machinery. Improved pressing techniques made solid eating chocolate commercially viable, and Baumeister adopted the process as soon as the equipment proved reliable. Drinking chocolate remained on the catalogue, but molded chocolate bars, blocks, and wrapped squares steadily overtook it in sales volume.

The Baumeister household grew during this same period. Evangeline was born in 1853, Rowena in 1856, Dieter in 1858, and Felix in 1862. The children grew up inside the business. Delivery carts rattled past their windows, factory problems were discussed over breakfast, and cooling trays were a constant feature of the household kitchen. Evangeline showed an early, serious interest in the factory floor; Rowena gravitated toward retail presentation and customer tastes; Dieter preferred watching the mechanics and engines; and Felix was fascinated by unusual ingredients and visitors from other ports.

Matilda also left a lasting practical imprint on the company's flavor profile. She planted almond trees on family property in the East Bay, supplying the kitchen with fresh California nuts. The resulting almond bars and squares sold so reliably that later company historians often assumed the combination had been in the family since Augsburg.

By the early 1870s, Baumeister Confections was an established, profitable manufacturer. It had permanent factory foremen, dependable supply lines, wholesale accounts across the western states, and an export trade through Pacific ports. Hieronymus spent his days in the workshop testing new machinery, while Matilda kept the firm's ledgers balanced and its credit clean. The company was finally secure enough to take creative risks without gambling its survival on every batch.

Part IV: The Last Experiments (1874 - 1879)
By the mid-1870s, Hieronymus was nearing sixty. The business was stable and Brickhouse Square was running smoothly, but he showed very little interest in slowing down. European chocolate houses were developing the first reliable methods for blending dairy solids into chocolate liquor, creating a smoother, milder bar that softened cacao's natural bitterness. The process fascinated Hieronymus, and he immediately ordered test equipment to experiment with California dairy supplies.

The factory test room became a testing ground for anything he could source from incoming cargo ships: tropical fruit extracts, unusual spices, toasted nuts, and experimental cream blends. Some of these formulas made it onto the production schedule. Others were scratched out after a single tasting and dumped into the scrap bins.

He took to labeling these experimental batches "Exotics." It was not an official marketing term at the time; Matilda mostly considered it his private shorthand for any test that ran over budget, took up too many cooling tables, or left the room smelling of roasted spices. But the name remained on his working folders.

One particular recipe gave him endless trouble: Lemon Ginger Milk Chocolate Swirls. The acidity of the lemon oil and the fiery heat of the ginger repeatedly clashed with the milk chocolate base, breaking the texture or completely masking the cacao. His test notes from 1878 show constant adjustments to ginger ratios, trials with candied peel, and warnings about ambient room humidity. Beside one entry, he scribbled, "Ginger's about right now. Lemon still cuts straight through it. Try the peel only next time." A few weeks later, another note reads, "Much better. Leave the ginger alone and cut the lemon again."

He kept tinkering with the proportions right through the following summer. Hieronymus had spent his entire life treating a bad batch as an instruction manual for the next attempt, and he saw no reason to stop just because the company had offices and a hundred employees on the payroll. Matilda kept the books steady, and the children were accustomed to being handed tasting spoons whenever their father emerged from the back room.

The lemon-ginger formula was still sitting on his bench when Hieronymus died suddenly on 3 September 1879, aged sixty-four. His death left the company without the central figure who had made every final operational decision since 1838. Matilda still held the ledgers and understood the business completely, and all four children were old enough to have strong ideas about how the company should move forward. Unfortunately, those ideas were about to pull the family in opposite directions.

The unfinished recipe for Lemon Ginger Milk Chocolate Swirls was filed away with his working notebooks. It would sit in the safe for decades - a collection of crossed-out weights and penciled corrections from a founder who worked right up until his last day.

The Family Fracture
Compiled by the Historical Archival Division of Baumeister Confections, 1946.

Part I: After Hieronymus (1879)
When Hieronymus died in September 1879, Baumeister Confections had to find out what it was without him. For forty-one years, he had been the final arbiter on everything from factory machinery to recipe tweaks. Matilda still held the commercial reins, knowing the accounts, contracts, and shipping agents better than anyone, but keeping four young adult siblings working as a team proved far more difficult than balancing a ledger.

Evangeline was twenty-six, Rowena twenty-three, Dieter twenty, and Felix seventeen. Evangeline had worked closely with her father on the factory floor and felt personally responsible for protecting his recipe standards and the family name. Rowena saw things differently. She believed the company was becoming sluggish and overly attached to tradition. She wanted modern advertising, wider wholesale distribution, bolder retail packaging, and a willingness to sell off dormant recipes that were generating no income.

Their early arguments sounded like standard commercial disputes: whether to retire a slow-selling bar, whether premium Caribbean cacao justified higher shipping rates, or whether to buy new machinery immediately or wait a quarter. But the tension went deeper. Evangeline thought Rowena was reckless with the firm's hard-won reputation, while Rowena felt Evangeline used her position as the eldest daughter to block any idea she had not thought of herself.

Dieter stayed out of the arguments whenever possible, preferring the quiet routine of the machinery rooms. Felix, still a teenager, found the shouting exhausting and had no interest in serving as a tiebreaker. Matilda spent that autumn keeping the factory running while constantly reminding her daughters that their father had been in the ground for barely three months and the business did not need to be reinvented before winter.

Into this fragile situation stepped Esteban Grimaldo. A smooth, well-connected figure in San Francisco commercial circles, Esteban possessed everything Rowena found lacking in her family: he was polished, ambitious, and enthusiastic about her commercial ideas. He spoke the language of contracts, licensing, and brand leverage, and he never prefaced an opinion by asking what Hieronymus would have done.

Matilda initially treated him as just another commercial acquaintance, and Evangeline had no immediate reason to suspect anything worse than an ambitious suitor. But over the closing months of 1879, Esteban became a fixture in Rowena's corner, providing business advice and encouraging her belief that her family was unfairly holding her back.

Part II: Two Sisters, Two Futures (Late 1879)
By December, the rift between Evangeline and Rowena was affecting daily operations. Evangeline wanted to steady the firm, protect existing supplier relationships, and keep production focused on proven quality. Rowena argued that the Baumeister name had tremendous untapped value that could be monetized through licensing, outside partnerships, and aggressive marketing.

Rowena's instincts were not entirely wrong. She understood retail display, gift packaging, and seasonal merchandising far better than Evangeline, and several of her packaging ideas eventually became standard practice. But Evangeline feared losing control. A Baumeister formula manufactured by a careless licensee would ruin decades of customer trust, and once recipe rights were sold, they could never be recalled. She refused to treat their father's recipe books as mere assets to be liquidated.

Matilda spent hours trying to bring the discussions back to basic accounting. She demanded cost sheets and revenue projections for Rowena's advertising schemes, and she demanded concrete figures from Evangeline whenever she wanted to reject a lucrative wholesale contract. But the arguments kept drifting from numbers into personal grievances.

Esteban Grimaldo used those grievances skillfully. He introduced Rowena to outside merchants and legal brokers, showed her how recipe licensing could be structured to generate immediate cash, and fed her frustration that the family treated her like an inexperienced junior partner. Rowena welcomed having someone take her commercial ambitions seriously.

Evangeline's distrust of Esteban grew by the week. She noticed that he spoke about Baumeister Confections as though he already had an equity stake in it, and she disliked how often Rowena's proposals arrived sounding word-for-word like Esteban's talking points. By the start of the new year, family dinners had ended. The two sisters communicated through brief office notes, and Esteban was spending nearly every working day in Rowena's office.

Part III: Jarrah, Esteban, and the Rift (1880)
The conflict soon spilled over into the family's Pacific trade connections. Arthur “Jarrah” Tangye, a Hong Kong merchant and shipping agent, had worked with Baumeister for years and had become central to their Pacific supply chain. He understood international trade routes, harbor politics, and commercial credit across Asian and Australian ports. He and Evangeline had also formed a deep personal bond, and the family expected them to marry before long.

The archival record from early 1880 shows that their relationship came under deliberate strain. A network of manufactured rumors, intercepted correspondence, and bad-faith business reports led each to believe the other had broken trust. One of Evangeline's former apprentices later admitted to carrying false messages, and correspondence recovered during the 1880 restoration proved Esteban had actively worked to drive Jarrah away from San Francisco.

Under the weight of constant corporate infighting and fabricated accusations, the relationship fractured. Jarrah stepped back from Baumeister affairs and returned to his shipping operations in Hong Kong. Evangeline dealt with the heartbreak by throwing herself completely into the factory floor, becoming harder, colder, and even more unyielding on matters of company control.

Rowena, meanwhile, married Esteban Grimaldo in a quiet civil ceremony. With that marriage, Esteban gained formal legal standing over Rowena's share of the family business. He immediately began treating that position as authority over the company as a whole.

Part IV: The Break (1880)
The break came when Rowena and Esteban began executing third-party contracts without the full Board's consent. They licensed selected Baumeister formulas to outside confectioners in regional ports, taking upfront cash advances. On paper, it was presented as an expansion strategy; in practice, it was a quick way to generate liquidity.

The factory floor at Brickhouse Square fell into chaos. Foremen received contradictory orders from Evangeline and Esteban. Suppliers held up shipments because bills were disputed. Export accounts were neglected, and regional operations began losing money. When creditors demanded payment, Esteban's solution was simple: sell more proprietary assets. Long-term licenses were converted to outright sales, and formulas that had not sold well in California were assigned to outside retailers to clear short-term debt.

This was how the Baumeister recipe collection was scattered across the globe. It was not a single catastrophic auction; it was a slow bleed across dozens of transactions. Recipes were traded for flour and sugar deliveries, pledged as loan collateral, or carried off by former managers who recognized that the family was too divided to take them to court. Within months, formulas perfected over decades in Augsburg, Sydney, and San Francisco were being produced by strangers who had no connection to the Baumeister family.

Evangeline saw the sales as pure desecration. Rowena saw Evangeline's stubbornness as the root cause of the cash crisis. The sisters stopped speaking entirely. Dieter quietly withdrew to overseas trading accounts, Felix avoided Headquarters, and Matilda found herself spending her days fending off creditors and trying to protect what little remained of the company's core assets.

Esteban moved with total impunity. He held meetings in the company boardroom, signed letters as executive manager, and referred to the factory as "his house." To Matilda and Evangeline, watching an outside opportunist dismantle Hieronymus's legacy while claiming to own it was unbearable.

By late 1880, Baumeister Confections had broken into pieces. Several overseas branches were shuttered, Brickhouse Square was running at a fraction of its capacity, and the family was completely estranged. Evangeline was alone in San Francisco, holding a handful of basic formulas and an empty ledger, facing the reality that everything her parents had built was gone.

That was when she decided to take a gamble of her own.

The First Restoration
Compiled by the Historical Archival Division of Baumeister Confections, 1946.

Part I: Evangeline's Gamble
By late 1880, Evangeline knew that family meetings would never fix what had been broken. Matilda was doing what she could to maintain the firm's legal shell, but the recipes, the production contracts, and the retail network were scattered across three continents. Bringing back those assets required someone who could operate without being dragged down by the family feud.

Her solution was to hire an unknown, independent Chocolatier. The apprentice she chose had no ties to Esteban, no stake in the inheritance, and virtually no capital. Evangeline started them from nothing, handing over a single case of chocolate to sell in San Francisco to establish a working cash balance, followed by the formula for a basic chocolate bar. She taught the apprentice how to buy market ingredients, set a factory production run, find retail buyers, and balance their travel overhead. Her journal from those weeks is characteristically practical: the new operator was tested step by step to see if they had the spine and the head for business.

An outside operator gave Evangeline a distinct advantage. Across the confectionery world, the Baumeister name had become complicated. Some merchants blamed Rowena; others had bought formulas from Esteban in good faith; many simply refused to deal with the family while lawsuits were threatened. An independent maker could walk into a market stall, buy supplies, and negotiate for recipes without forcing everyone in the room to choose a side in the Baumeister family war.

After the apprentice proved their capability with a successful sales run to New York, Evangeline laid out the full scope of the project. The family's recipes were scattered across international ports, and she did not want them recovered merely to be locked in a filing cabinet. She backed the Chocolatier to build a brand-new commercial chocolate venture using those recovered formulas. She provided operating funds, conferred the rank of Novice, and had the apprentice register an independent company name and brand.

This was a deliberate strategy. The Chocolatier was not appointed an officer of the old firm, nor were they handed Baumeister Confections. They were building an operational enterprise that could reopen abandoned factories, secure raw ingredients, and prove that the Baumeister recipes were still commercially dominant when handled with discipline. Every operational factory and recovered recipe proved to the trade that the Baumeister heritage still had immense value.

Part II: Recipes on the Road (1880)
As the Chocolatier began traveling, it quickly became apparent that "scattered recipes" was an understatement. The formulas had diffused across the global economy. Some were held by respectable confectioners; others had been traded between merchants to settle debts; some were tucked away in private vaults. In San Francisco, a Barbary Coast saloonkeeper casually admitted he had accepted an old Baumeister recipe to settle an outstanding bar tab.

Securing these recipes required completely different approaches in every port. Some holders wanted cash; some demanded high-volume shipments of finished chocolate; others simply wanted proof that the buyer knew how to make the confection properly. Personal introductions were everything. A contact in London led to a trader in Trinidad, which led in turn to the New York Public Library, where the head archivist held several rare Baumeister formulas in a private vault. Evangeline's old working relationship with him was close enough that a brief note from her - "unleash the dog" - was all it took to grant the Chocolatier access.

Recovering a recipe was only half the battle; manufacturing it was the real test. Advanced truffles and specialty bars required rare ingredients that could not be bought from standard wholesalers. Specific cacao beans had to be purchased directly from plantations in Merida, Costa Rica, and Trinidad, while items like pure vanillin or almond paste had to be sourced through specific trading ports. To keep production moving, the Chocolatier had to rebuild an international supply line from scratch.

The company's former factories told the same story. Several brick facilities that had once flown the Baumeister banner sat dark or were being run into the ground by local receivers. The Chocolatier bought these facilities back one by one, repairing steam pipes, cleaning molds, and hiring local foremen. Evangeline watched this expansion with pride, noting that her father's industrial vision was being rebuilt by someone who had earned every foot of floor space.

As the Chocolatier's reputation spread, the search gained momentum. Distant relatives were relieved to see the formulas back in production, merchants offered leads on formulas held in other cities, and shopkeepers sought out the Chocolatier directly because their finished cases were consistently superior to local competitors. By mid-1880, an operation that had started with a single case of chocolate in San Francisco had become an international enterprise with operations across North America, Europe, and the Caribbean.

And everywhere the Chocolatier traveled, they heard the other side of the family story. What had begun as Evangeline's account of sibling betrayal was looking more and more like a calculated corporate takeover engineered from the shadows.

Part III: What Really Happened (1880)
As the Chocolatier reconnected with old Baumeister partners, the portrait of Rowena as a simple, heartless villain began to fall apart. She had signed disastrous contracts and sold away the company's heritage, but traders who had dealt with her during that period kept pointing to Esteban Grimaldo. Witnesses described a marriage that had turned deeply controlling, with Grimaldo isolating Rowena from her relatives while pushing the asset sales through his own broker network.

Esteban soon confirmed those suspicions through his own actions. As the Chocolatier began buying up former Baumeister factories and securing key ingredient lines, Grimaldo surfaced to threaten them directly. He warned them away from "his company," sent hired hands to intimidate suppliers, and openly threatened to destroy ingredient shipments. His claims of ownership were absurd; he had married into the family months after Hieronymus died, yet he spoke as if he had built the enterprise with his own hands.

The Chocolatier also uncovered the truth regarding Jarrah Tangye. Family friends in San Francisco confirmed that Evangeline and Jarrah had been deeply in love, and that Grimaldo had systematically forged notes, delayed shipping messages, and paid off third parties to manufacture a bitter estrangement between them. When a direct letter from Grimaldo to Rowena was recovered and delivered to Felix Baumeister, Felix recognized the handwriting and confirmed what Evangeline had refused to believe: Esteban had deliberately engineered the rift to remove Jarrah's steady commercial influence from the firm.

Serving as an independent go-between, the Chocolatier began repairing the damage. They delivered twelve cases of Almond Vanilla Truffles to Jarrah in Hong Kong - the exact recipe Evangeline had made for him years before. Jarrah recognized the gesture immediately. He sent twelve cases of Coffee Cinnamon Truffles back to San Francisco with a personal message, breaking months of painful silence. For the first time in over a year, Evangeline and Jarrah were writing to each other directly instead of through intermediaries.

Meanwhile, Rowena's situation with Esteban had collapsed completely. Grimaldo's abusive temper, his reckless commercial debts, and the undeniable paper trail proving his deception finally gave Rowena the clarity she needed. She broke with him permanently in Sydney. Grimaldo reacted with bitter fury, railing against the Chocolatier for stripping away everything he had planned to control. With his legal authority severed and his schemes exposed, Esteban Grimaldo vanished from the family's business affairs for good.

Rowena was finally free, but she was broke, isolated, and carrying the burden of having brought her family's company to the brink of ruin. She knew an apology on paper was completely worthless. If she was ever to face her family again, she would have to prove her remorse in chocolate.

Part IV: The Peace Offering (1880)
In Sydney, a devastated Rowena Baumeister met with the Chocolatier. She admitted her catastrophic mistakes and confessed that the very recipes she needed to make amends were no longer in her possession. She asked the Chocolatier to manufacture the favorite confections of the family members she had harmed most, using her remaining funds to secure the missing formulas.

Dieter was reached in Istanbul with fifty cases of his favorite Milk Blend Truffles, recovered through trade contacts in Sydney. Felix was found in Trinidad, accepting fifty cases of Blend Mint Coffee Truffles after the recipe was tracked through Accra. Both brothers forgave her without hesitation, offering their blessings and helping the Chocolatier locate the next formulas on the list.

Making peace with Jarrah carried deeper stakes. His favorite confection was Raspberry Coconut Truffles, a recipe that had been sold off during the crisis. In recovering it, the Chocolatier confronted the former apprentice who had carried Grimaldo's fabricated letters. Overcome with guilt, the apprentice surrendered the formula. The Chocolatier manufactured fifty cases and delivered them to Jarrah in Hong Kong. Jarrah accepted the peace offering, wrote back to forgive Rowena, and gave his full blessing to the restoration.

That left Evangeline. When Rowena had been forced to liquidate the recipe collection, there was one formula she had hidden away beyond Esteban's reach: Extra Dark Limited Stock Blended Cacao Truffles, Evangeline's personal favorite. Rowena had deposited the formula with a trusted harbor clerk at Sydney Quay for safekeeping. It was an exceptionally demanding recipe, requiring high-grade varietal cacaos from across the Caribbean and Central America. Rowena asked the Chocolatier to manufacture one hundred cases and deliver them to San Francisco as her ultimate plea for forgiveness.

When the shipment arrived at Brickhouse Square, Evangeline understood immediately. The truffles could not restore the lost years or undo the public humiliation, but Rowena had preserved their family's crown jewel when she had nothing else left, and she had trusted Evangeline's own apprentice to make it. Evangeline accepted the gift, declared the bitter feud finished, and embraced the sister she had thought was lost forever.

In recognition of an extraordinary achievement, Evangeline conferred upon the player the title of Master Chocolatier. It was a title earned through genuine mastery. In less than a year, an unknown apprentice had traveled the globe, restored sixty-four scattered recipes, reopened six closed factories, built a flourishing commercial supply chain, exposed a predatory interloper, and brought an estranged family back to the table.

Baumeister Confections did not return to its old form overnight. Some factories were now owned by the Chocolatier's independent firm, and the family had learned hard lessons about trust, legal contracts, and corporate governance. But the recipes were safe, the kilns were hot, and the Baumeister name once again stood for the finest chocolate in the world.

The Rebuilding Years
Compiled by the Historical Archival Division of Baumeister Confections, 1946.

Part I: A Family Again (1881 - 1904)
The reconciliation of 1880 allowed the Baumeisters to return to normal commercial life. There were still tangled contracts to sort out and damaged wholesale accounts to mend, but family dinners resumed without someone walking out the door. Evangeline Baumeister and Arthur “Jarrah” Tangye took time to rebuild their relationship on solid ground, marrying in San Francisco on 14 June 1881. Their children - Joseph, Lillian, and Victor - followed over the next decade.

Jarrah's formal return solidified the company's Pacific trade lines. As a skilled merchant, translator, and freight coordinator with strong connections through Hong Kong, Sydney, and San Francisco, he understood maritime logistics intuitively. Evangeline set recipe standards and production discipline; Jarrah ensured raw beans, vanilla, and sugar moved through customs and freight holds without delay. His expertise anchored the firm's global trade for a generation.

The company's commercial structure was unique. The Master Chocolatier of 1880 had built a thriving independent manufacturing firm using recovered Baumeister recipes and reopened factories. Rather than trying to absorb that company, Baumeister Confections maintained a close operational alliance with it. Recipes, raw supplies, and factory capacity were shared by mutual agreement. It was an unconventional corporate structure, but after surviving near-total destruction, the family preferred practical success over rigid corporate paperwork.

Internal responsibilities settled naturally. Evangeline served as the authority on recipe integrity, ingredient quality, and the family name. Dieter Baumeister took charge of plant operations, boiler maintenance, and output efficiency. Felix Baumeister leaned toward creative experimentation, showing a keen interest in unusual botanicals and laying the groundwork for the company's eventual expansion into coffee.

Rowena returned to the family circle with genuine humility. The family forgave her, but no one forgot the devastation of 1879. She retained her financial share, but any contracts involving trademarks, licensing, or outside capital were subjected to strict Board scrutiny. Rowena accepted this balance willingly, contributing retail presentation ideas and shop concepts while leaving governance to her siblings.

Matilda Baumeister remained the elder anchor of the firm throughout this era. Having built the company alongside Hieronymus, she insisted that the lessons of the collapse be permanently recorded in standard operating rules. Trademark assignments were locked down, licensing was outlawed, foreign shop foremen were bound by strict written charters, and monthly ledger reviews became mandatory. Matilda passed away peacefully in San Francisco on 4 December 1896, aged seventy-seven. She left behind a stable, profitable company that no longer relied on the whims of a single patriarch to survive.

By the turn of the century, the company operated confidently as Baumeister Confections International. The business was profitable and international, but Evangeline had begun questioning their traditional expansion model. Building enormous, multi-story brick factories in foreign ports required massive capital and left the firm vulnerable to regional downturns. She wondered if a compact retail outlet could manufacture custom, artisanal chocolate on site, using small-scale, steam-powered machinery.

In 1904, the Board backed her to test the concept. The company commissioned an eccentric Swiss-German engineer named Klaus Werner to design a suite of compact chocolate machines. Evangeline volunteered to personally test this experimental equipment in the most remote, climatically demanding locations she could find.

Part II: The Remote-Shop Experiment (1904 - 1905)
Evangeline arrived in Iquitos, Peru, in August 1904 with the first set of compact steam machinery. Amazonian heat and extreme humidity provided the ultimate trial. If chocolate could be tempered and poured inside a small storefront here without spoiling, it could work anywhere. The machinery held up remarkably well, locals loved the interactive experience of watching chocolate made behind the counter, and the shop proved profitable within weeks.

Klaus Werner stayed in close communication by wire. At first, his inquiries focused strictly on steam pressure, valve tolerances, and cooling times. But by October, his telegrams began probing into the exact varieties of local cacao, fruits, and vanilla Evangeline was sourcing from local river traders. Evangeline answered casually, assuming an engineer was naturally curious about what went into his hoppers.

The next field trial opened in Grytviken, South Georgia, in November 1904, trading Amazonian humidity for sub-Antarctic cold. Here, Evangeline partnered with Klara Gunbjorg Larsen, a tough, resourceful local who understood the settlement's whaling community. Klaus upgraded the installation with a mechanized topping dispenser and a small steam-powered delivery Zeppelin to move parcels across icy terrain. By February 1905, Klara took over permanent management of the Grytviken shop under an official Baumeister partnership charter, proving that remote retail shops could thrive under trusted local ownership.

Part III: Higher, Colder, Hotter (1905)
Evangeline reached Namche Bazaar, Nepal, on 15 April 1905, setting up equipment at eleven thousand feet above sea level. The Himalayan air was thin and freezing, testing how atmospheric pressure affected boiling points and steam engines. The machinery adapted without issue. Evangeline brought in local cherries, walnuts, and honey, partnering with Pemba Gelu, an astute Himalayan merchant who quickly mastered the equipment.

Klaus continued sending updates, adding a moving sample conveyor belt to keep waiting customers entertained during peak morning rushes. But on 9 June, Evangeline noted in her journal that Klaus's telegrams were becoming unusually persistent about proprietary ingredient ratios and source locations. He cared very little about mechanical wear, but repeatedly demanded details on Pemba's dried fruit and nut suppliers. Evangeline noted the behavior with growing unease.

By late June, with Pemba managing the Namche shop, Evangeline traveled to the tropical heat of Krakatoa, Indonesia. Volcanic ash, sea air, and sweltering temperatures pushed the machinery to its limits. Once again, the equipment ran cleanly. Partnering with Ayu Korowati, Evangeline introduced local cashew nuts, coconut cream, and dulce de leche to the compact line, turning the beachside shop into a bustling trade hub.

Klaus had already traveled ahead to Kamchatka to prepare the next site. When he wired asking specifically about the fat content of Ayu's coconut supplier, Evangeline realized that every unique regional ingredient she touched was being logged by her engineer.

She arrived at the Kamchatka Peninsula on 3 October 1905 amid early blizzards. Partnering with Nadia Starvo, she set up the shop using regional pine nuts and imported saffron. But the mechanical tests were no longer her primary concern. She had received a disturbing dispatch from San Francisco: Schokolade Weltreich, the aggressive German confectionery conglomerate, had just launched a new product line using the exact unusual ingredients Evangeline had tested in Nepal and Indonesia. The leak had to be internal.

Part IV: Russian Cashews (1905)
Evangeline handled the betrayal with characteristic sharpness. Instead of confronting Klaus Werner directly and giving him a chance to flee or cover his tracks, she decided to hand him an obvious bait line. On 26 October 1905, she sent Klaus an urgent, confidential telegram claiming she had discovered an extraordinary wild crop in the Siberian foothills: Russian Cashews.

Cashews are strictly tropical; they do not grow in sub-Arctic Russia. If Klaus was an honest engineer, he would have pointed out the botanical absurdity. If he was selling company secrets to Schokolade Weltreich, he would pass the trade name along immediately.

The trap snapped shut on 30 November. Baumeister trading contacts in Hamburg and London reported that Schokolade Weltreich agents had begun frantically circulating inquiries across Baltic ports trying to buy exclusive import rights for "Russian Cashews."

Evangeline attempted to wire Klaus Werner for an explanation, but he had already abandoned his workshop and disappeared into continental Europe. Yet Evangeline refused to scrap his work. Klaus was a thief and an industrial spy, but his mechanical engineering was undeniably brilliant. The compact dispensers, automated topping trays, Zeppelin lines, and steam boilers had survived the most brutal climates on earth without a single catastrophic failure. The equipment belonged to Baumeister Confections, and Evangeline was determined to finish the project on her own terms.

After transferring the Kamchatka shop to Nadia Starvo, Evangeline returned to San Francisco for the winter holidays. By March 1906, after a brief rest with Jarrah, she set out for the final proving ground: the scorching sands of the Gaberoun Oasis in Libya.

Part V: Without Klaus (1906)
The trials at Gaberoun in March 1906 were designed as an operational stress test. Headquarters set up a series of rigorous benchmarks, awarding $1,000 in equipment development funds for every commercial target Evangeline met without Klaus on site. She had to operate in blistering desert heat without letting inventory soften, serve crowds of local traders without running out of tempered stock, and manage high-volume delivery runs on strict timetables.

Some conservative voices in San Francisco argued that the machines should be mothballed simply because Klaus had designed them. Evangeline brushed the objections aside. The machines were tools paid for with company capital, and in the Libyan heat, they operated flawlessly. On 30 March 1906, the Gaberoun shop cleared $3,000 in daily sales, serving over thirty customers an hour during peak trading.

The remote-shop experiment proved that Baumeister Confections could expand without building massive brick factories in every territory. Compact, locally managed shops could manufacture premium, small-batch chocolate anywhere on earth, adapting to regional flavors while maintaining strict Baumeister standards. Evangeline returned home with an expanded ingredient catalogue, six thriving international partnerships, and an enterprise that was ready for the modern century.

The Spirit of Innovation
Compiled by the Historical Archival Division of Baumeister Confections, 1946.

Part I: The Next Generation (1906 - 1924)
Following the Gaberoun trials, Baumeister Confections entered a period of steady corporate consolidation. Evangeline gradually stepped back from exhausting field expeditions, taking her place alongside Dieter, Felix, and Rowena on the Board of Directors. Daily executive management transferred to her eldest son, Joseph Arthur Tangye.

Joseph had grown up in the shadow of the 1880 collapse. He remembered the unpaid bills, the family estrangement, and the immense labor it had taken his mother to rebuild the company's reputation. As a result, Joseph operated with heavy caution. He favored established retail lines, long-term wholesale agreements, and strict cash reserves. He and his wife, Elena Vittoria Bellini Tangye, raised three children in San Francisco: Zachariah, Alexandra, and Loudon. Elena served as the steady social balance in the family, maintaining harmony while Joseph focused on balance sheets.

Their daughter Alexandra inherited her grandmother Evangeline's fire. Growing up around the Brickhouse Square factory, she saw innovation not as an occasional luxury, but as the only reason the company had survived this long. By the early 1920s, the confectionery market was changing rapidly. The post-war Roaring Twenties brought jazz, consumer travel, modern retail displays, and shifting tastes. Companies that relied on forty-year-old chocolate bar formulas were watching their market share dwindle.

Alex pleaded with her father to modernize the catalogue, experiment with new ingredients, and invest in creative product development. Joseph refused. He viewed her proposals as the same kind of reckless overreach that had ruined Rowena in 1879. The company was profitable, his balance sheets were clean, and he saw no reason to risk company capital on novelties.

Their professional dispute soon merged with a bitter personal one. Joseph began pressuring Alex to marry Christoph Moreno, an influential, polished figure in San Francisco commercial circles whom Joseph saw as an ideal business partner. Alex despised Christoph, recognizing his polished charm as an ambitious front, and gave her heart to Sean Fletcher, an honest, adventurous pilot. When Joseph dismissed Sean and insisted on Christoph, Alex decided she was done talking.

On 1 January 1925, Alexandra Tangye met with an independent Chocolatier in San Francisco to launch a secret corporate rebellion.

Part II: Words Aren't Working (1925)
Alex's plan was simple: words were not working on her father, so she would let financial returns do the talking. She partnered with the Chocolatier to build an agile, modern confectionery enterprise from scratch, completely off Baumeister's books. Alex provided operational guidance, secret recipes, and personal introductions, while the Chocolatier took the helm, managing factories, purchasing raw ingredients, and opening retail outlets across global ports.

Operating under the radar, the Chocolatier modernized production, introducing squares, delicate infusions, and rich nut pralines. Rather than relying on standard commercial wholesalers, they established direct relationships with growers in hidden trading ports - sourcing wild plantains and fire ants from the Amazon, anise and saffron from the Sahara, and lavender honey from the high Himalayas.

To turn these raw materials into market-ready confections, Alex directed the Chocolatier to acquire the Chocolate Tasting Laboratory in Buenos Aires, placing it under the direction of her eccentric cousin, Teddy Baumeister. The laboratory became a dedicated engine for recipe development. Here, unusual ingredients were blended, tested, and calibrated into balanced formulas, allowing the Chocolatier to launch successful new lines while large manufacturers were still drafting proposals.

The venture was a runaway commercial success, but secrecy could not last. In San Francisco, Joseph Tangye discovered the unauthorized enterprise, realized his own daughter was running it, and reacted with intense fury.

Part III: The Split and the Sabotage (1925)
When the Chocolatier returned to San Francisco Headquarters, they were confronted not by Alex, but by a cold, furious Joseph Tangye. Joseph informed them that Alex had been exiled from the family home, accused the pair of destabilizing the company, and ordered the Chocolatier to cut all ties with Baumeister Confections permanently.

Alex refused to surrender. Arranging a secret meeting at the foot of Mount Merapi in Jakarta, Indonesia, she informed the Chocolatier that retreat was impossible. Since Joseph refused to see reason and remained completely under Christoph Moreno's influence, they would take over Baumeister Confections through a formal Board vote. To do that, they needed to acquire the remaining independent shops, build a massive portfolio of luxury Truffles, and force the Board of Directors to recognize their operational dominance.

As the Chocolatier expanded operations, Christoph Moreno dropped all pretense of being a friendly suitor. Realizing his grip on the Tangye family was slipping, Christoph and his brother Tristan Moreno initiated an aggressive campaign of corporate sabotage. Tristan tricked the Chocolatier into a factory inspection in New York, using the distraction to vandalize cooling equipment and halt production lines. Elsewhere, Moreno operatives raided ingredient warehouses and attempted to bribe local port officials into delaying shipments.

Worse still, intelligence from European ports revealed that Christoph was secretly working as an asset for Schokolade Weltreich. His goal was never to help Baumeister Confections; he had intended to marry Alex, take control of the firm from the aging Joseph, and sell the company's assets to its German rival from within.

Part IV: The Five Signatures (1925)
With Christoph's hostility in the open, Alex moved toward the endgame. She sent the Chocolatier to Sydney to consult with her great-aunt Rowena Baumeister. Having lived through her own bitter fracture forty-five years earlier, Rowena offered invaluable perspective: being right was not enough; one had to build a bridge for the family to walk back across.

Rowena provided the blueprint for victory: the Exotics line. She handed over Hieronymus's unfinished notes for Lemon Ginger Milk Chocolate Swirls, challenging the Chocolatier to use Teddy's Buenos Aires laboratory to develop an entire range of twelve complex, luxury confections using ingredients sourced from the secret ports. The resulting Exotics represented the perfect union of Baumeister tradition and modern innovation.

Back in San Francisco, Elena Tangye uncovered definitive proof of Christoph Moreno's collusion with Schokolade Weltreich. Armed with letters and bank drafts, Elena confronted Joseph in his office, forcing him to face the reality of his preferred successor's treason. Shaken and deeply remorseful, Joseph authorized an immediate formal apology to Sean Fletcher, removing the final barrier between Alex and the man she loved.

With Moreno discredited, Alex initiated the formal Board challenge. To claim authority, the Chocolatier had to secure the signed endorsements of the five family Board members through specific, large-scale production deliveries:
• Evangeline Baumeister signed happily after receiving 50 cases of Lemon Ginger Milk Chocolate Swirls.
• Dieter Baumeister gave his endorsement upon delivery of 75 cases of Candied Orange Peels made with his own Costa Rican cacao.
• Felix Baumeister added his signature after a delivery of 100 cases each of Sweet Honey Hearts and Tea and Toasted Pecan Ivories.
• Rowena Baumeister endorsed the plan following a delivery of 200 cases of Spicy Chocolate Smooches, passing along a personal message to Sean Fletcher that solidified his reunion with Alex.

That left Joseph. To convince her father that this was an industrial reality rather than an arrogant fluke, Alex tasked the Chocolatier with manufacturing and delivering 100 cases of all 12 unique Exotic recipes - 1,200 cases in total - straight to San Francisco Headquarters.

Confronted by a warehouse full of flawless, innovative confections, Joseph conceded. Admitting his blindness regarding Christoph and his stubborn resistance to change, he signed the handover papers, apologized to his daughter in person, and officially confirmed the Chocolatier as Chief Executive Officer of Baumeister Confections.

The 1925 crisis established a modern truth for the firm: heritage provides authority, but only relentless, practical innovation keeps the doors open.

Through Depression and War
Compiled by the Historical Archival Division of Baumeister Confections, 1946.

Part I: A Modern Company (1926 - 1929)
The years following the 1925 reorganization were among the most productive in the company's history. With the player serving as Chief Executive Officer and Alexandra managing strategic expansion and product design, Baumeister Confections balanced operational stability with continuous creative output. The Buenos Aires laboratory became a permanent department, testing new flavor profiles and sourcing varietal cacaos across global trade routes.

Joseph Tangye remained on the Board of Directors. Once relieved of operational command, his financial instincts and cautious oversight proved genuinely valuable, serving as a practical check on ambitious capital expenditures. The family operated with shared purpose, recognizing that creative ambition and financial discipline were equally necessary.

Alex and Sean Fletcher were married shortly after the takeover, establishing their home in San Francisco. Sean's aviation background opened up rapid transport possibilities for high-value ingredients and diplomatic trade meetings. Their daughter, Margaret Evangeline Fletcher, was born in San Francisco on 2 April 1927, followed by their son, Thomas Joseph Fletcher, born in Zürich on 15 August 1929. By the close of the decade, Baumeister Confections was posting record global revenues.

Part II: The Depression (1929 - 1935)
The crash of October 1929 hit the luxury confectionery market with brutal force. Discretionary consumer spending collapsed, international credit froze, and retail demand for high-end Exotics and gift boxes dried up almost overnight. The worldwide deflationary spiral and subsequent international bank failures made basic freight and payroll difficult to maintain.

The company adapted swiftly. Rather than running up crippling debt, the Board mothballed idle machinery, suspended secondary production shifts, and focused resources on dependable, low-cost essentials like Basic Bars and Milk Chocolate Squares. Dieter and Chas Baumeister personally greased and sealed the specialized Exotics equipment, ensuring valuable production assets were preserved rather than sold off for scrap.

Joseph's strict financial conservatism became the company's lifeline during the 1933 Bank Holiday, keeping enough working capital on hand to keep the boilers fueled and core staff employed. By 1935, Baumeister Confections emerged from the worst of the economic slump intact, having protected its core factories and preserved its entire recipe portfolio.

Part III: A Wider World at War (1935 - 1945)
As global trade recovered in the late 1930s, the Board adopted a decentralized management structure. Alex's brother, Zachariah Tangye, established Morocco Fine Coffees in Tangier, developing it into an international coffee brokerage and laying the groundwork for the modern Special Orders system. Felix Baumeister intensified his coffee research in Cape Town, Dieter supervised manufacturing efficiency, and Whitney Baumeister assumed leadership over staff training, personnel welfare, and production logistics.

The outbreak of the Second World War in September 1939 shattered international shipping. U-boat campaigns in the Atlantic and naval blockades in the Mediterranean made global commodity transport extraordinarily dangerous. Sugar and dairy were placed under strict government rationing, and cacao imports fell to historic lows.

The company's factories diverged along geopolitical lines:
• The facilities in San Francisco, Toronto, Cape Town, and Wellington were converted to wartime contracts, producing emergency rations and military food packets for Allied forces.
• The Zürich factory, shielded by Swiss neutrality, served as a crucial diplomatic and financial clearinghouse, though raw cacao was nearly impossible to import through surrounding borders.
• The Tokyo operation went completely dark following the outbreak of the Pacific War in December 1941, cutting off all communication with San Francisco Headquarters for the duration of the conflict.

The Buenos Aires laboratory suspended operations as transatlantic shipping collapsed. The company survived, but by 1945 its global network was splintered, with machinery worn down, trade routes severed, and facilities sitting idle.

Part IV: Sean’s Last Flight (1943 - 1946)
The war brought personal devastation to the family. In early 1943, Sean Fletcher volunteered for active service in the United States Eighth Air Force, piloting B-24 Liberators on strategic daylight bombing runs over occupied Europe. Operating out of bases in eastern England alongside his wingman and close friend Thomas Hardy, Sean flew dozens of high-risk sorties.

In late 1944, during a deep penetration mission over central Germany, Sean's aircraft took catastrophic flak damage to its left wing and engine block. The bomber fell out of formation and spiraled into dense cloud cover. The official War Department report listed Captain Sean Fletcher as missing in action, presumed dead.

Thomas Hardy, however, swore under debriefing that he had seen a single white parachute open beneath the burning aircraft before it struck the tree line. Hardy's eyewitness report was quietly buried by the squadron's intelligence liaison officer - a cold, calculating German defector operating under Allied intelligence named Wolf Fleischer. Fleischer filed the report as "unconfirmed combat stress hallucination," officially closing the file.

Alex refused to accept the military's verdict. Knowing Sean's resourcefulness and trusting Hardy's account, she spent the final months of the war pressing government bureaus, military morgues, and POW repatriation camps for any trace of her husband. When official channels returned only form letters, Alex resolved to take the investigation into her own hands.

Part V: Splintered Again (1945 - 1946)
With the conclusion of hostilities in 1945, Baumeister Confections faced a daunting reconstruction effort. The company held valuable trademarks and real estate, but its supply lines were destroyed, its machinery sat idle, and its Board was scattered across the globe. Felix was experimenting with coffee roasting in Cape Town, Dieter was managing recovery in Tokyo, Joseph was restructuring finances in Toronto, and Evangeline was holding together the San Francisco headquarters.

Alex could not rebuild a splintered international corporation while simultaneously chasing wartime intelligence leads across Europe and the Americas. The dual burden was tearing her apart. Following family precedent, she decided to place company operations in the hands of a capable outside executive.

On 27 June 1946, in Zürich, Switzerland, Alexandra Fletcher formally recruited an outside candidate to take charge of Baumeister Confections. Entrusting the applicant with the immediate challenge of reopening the Zürich works and winning the endorsements of the Board of Directors, Alex packed her bags to follow up on a promising lead in the Southern Hemisphere.

For the Historical Archival Division, that is where this chronicle concludes.

The rest is current business.

My dearest Sean,

It is late, and the Zürich office is finally quiet. The Board was relentless today. Felix wants to talk about African coffee routes, Dieter is philosophizing about factory efficiency, and my father… well, he is trying his best. But the weight of this company has never felt heavier.

They expect me to lead our post-war recovery. They want me to smile, to shake hands, to rebuild. But how can I rebuild an empire when my own world is in pieces?

The military brass told me again today that I need to move on. They said your plane went down, that the mission was classified, and that I need to accept the inevitable. But I know you, Sean Fletcher. You are far too stubborn to just fade away into some jungle. I feel it in my very soul - you are still out there.

I made a decision today that would probably give Grandmother Evangeline a heart attack. I hired an outsider. Someone to take over the day-to-day operations of the company. It is a massive gamble, but I see a spark in them. They remind me of myself back in '25, when we first fought my father to save this business.

I have to trust them to keep the factories running, because tomorrow, I am leaving. I have secured a diplomatic passport and I have a whisper of a lead in Australia. I don't care how far I have to travel, who I have to bribe, or what shadows I have to step into.

Hold on, my love. Wherever you are, just hold on. I am coming.

Yours always,
Alex

Felix Baumeister's Coffee Notebook
Selected working notes from the Cape Town Works, 1945–1946.

18 November 1945
Well, the drum turns. That is about the only praise I can offer it today.

The south-easter came howling off the bay around noon and blew soot right back down the burner pipe. The front bearing squeals like a pig every time I load more than ten pounds, and when I pulled the Santos lot out at quarter past two, half the batch was the color of an old boot and the other half was still greenish-yellow and smelled like hay. Inedible.

Chocolate is forgiving. If cacao misbehaves on the rollers, you can usually conche it, temper it, or nurse it along until it behaves. Coffee doesn't negotiate. Turn your back for sixty seconds to oil a gear and the whole charge goes up in smoke.

Need an exhaust hood that actually drafts, and a slower pulley on the belt.
(Note in margin: Chas wired from San Francisco to ask if I've burned the wharf down yet. Did not reply.)

7 January 1946
Progress. Not perfection, but progress.

Alice rehung the flue pipe with a damper we can adjust from the bench, which keeps the draft from blowing the flame flat every time the warehouse doors open. The bigger breakthrough was shutting my mouth and listening. Coffee makes a racket in the drum once it gets up to heat - a sharp, wooden crack like dry twigs snapping underfoot. Alice heard it before I did. Once that snapping starts, the bean doubles in size, the chaff blows off into the collector, and the roast changes color with every turn of the wheel.

Pull it ten seconds too early and it tastes like sour grass. Leave it twenty seconds too long and you might as well scrape ashes off the boiler grate into a cup.

The grinder is my next headache. If the burrs are set too tight, it turns the beans into powder that turns to mud the instant hot water hits it - harsh enough to strip paint. Back the plates off a fraction and it cracks into gravel, and then the brew runs out looking like pale dishwater. Finding the middle ground took four hours and half a sack of Brazilian beans. My hands are shaking from tasting so much of it.

26 February 1946
Ran trials all morning with milk, cream, and three different cane sugars from Natal.

Tried to salvage an over-roasted batch by dumping a quarter-pint of cream and four spoons of sugar into the mug. A total waste of dairy. Now it just tastes like burnt lumber floating in sweet milk. Shani used to scold me for doing that with chocolate ganache when I was forty years younger: "Felix, if the foundation is crooked, more paint won't straighten the walls." She was right, of course. She usually was.

I miss having her across the table to take one sip, make a terrible face at me, and tell me plainly to throw it in the gutter and start over.

The lesson stands: the roast has to be clean before it ever meets a cow. If a customer needs three lumps of sugar just to endure the bitterness, we haven't made coffee. We've made a punishment.

19 April 1946
Three identical roasts today. Three.

We loaded the drum, brought the temp up slow, caught the crack at nine minutes, and dumped the charge onto the cooling tray with the suction fan running. Every batch came out the color of roasted chestnuts, completely dry, smelling of toasted bread and dark cocoa. Alice stood over the tray with me, stirring the beans with a wooden paddle so they wouldn't keep cooking themselves from their own heat, and neither of us said a word until the beans were cool to the touch.

The Cape Town crew have worked wonders on this floor. Half of my original drawings were mechanical nonsense that would have rattled itself to pieces by Christmas, but Alice and the fitters quietly corrected the brackets, tightened the pulleys, and built something that actually repeats itself.

Now the machinery is ready. The problem is the beans.

Most of what docks in the harbor right now is robusta or rough, bulk commercial stock meant for ships' galleys. It has plenty of caffeine and almost no character. If the Baumeister name is going onto a tin, the cup has to taste like something worth sitting down for.

3 June 1946
Good correspondence yesterday from the islands.

I've been writing to a plantation contact in Kona, Hawaii - a grower named Kalei Kamalaninui up the slopes from the bay, and a merchant fellow, Hekili, who handles the open-air market down near the wharf. The sample parcel they shipped via the Pacific mail packet finally arrived this morning.

Remarkable beans. Large, even, perfectly dry. I roasted a half-pound in the sample pan over a spirit burner just to see what was there.

Zero harshness. It has this clean, nutty sweetness that sits on the tongue without that sharp, sour bite I've been fighting in the African lots. It doesn't need to be masked. It doesn't need six varieties of spice to cover its flaws.

I wrote back to Hawaii this afternoon asking for a regular shipment of their Kona beans, and told Alice to source fresh dairy cream and white cane sugar for the factory stock. We start simple: Cup A Joe. Just pure Kona coffee, rich cream, and sugar. No elaborate spice work, no liqueurs, no wild Felix Baumeister experiments using dried petals and roots from five different ports.

Not yet, anyway.

Let's show the family that we can brew an honest cup first. Once the Board sees people paying good money for it, then we can start having some fun.

BAUMEISTER CONFECTIONS INTERNATIONAL
Chocolate Tasting Laboratory - Buenos Aires
Temporary Suspension and Inventory Record - 17 August 1942

Reason for suspension: Total disruption of commercial Atlantic shipping routes, municipal power and fuel restrictions, unavailability of replacement brass fittings and conche gaskets from overseas, and inability to maintain consistent consignments of experimental ingredients.

Laboratory status: CLOSED TO ROUTINE DEVELOPMENT WORK

Staff retained: 4 (maintenance and dry storage oversight)
Staff reassigned: 11 (transferred to regional commercial accounts or released)
Active formulation trials halted: 27
Completed formula books placed in storage: 9 volumes

Equipment
Two small experimental tempering kettles drained, coated with mineral tallow to protect against River Plate humidity, and covered with oiled canvas.
One laboratory cocoa-butter press drained, pressure valves relieved, and grease-packed.
Three bench grinders dismantled; adjustment collars greased and wired in neutral alignment.
Six copper tasting pans scrubbed dry and locked in Cabinet B.
Analytical balance scales disassembled; agate knife-edge bearings wrapped in lint-free flannel and boxed separately from brass gram weights.
Glassware washed, dried, and crated in wood shavings. Six pipettes broken during packing; replacements unavailable.

Handwritten in margin: Whoever shoved the Baumé hydrometers into the drawer with the heavy copper spatulas owes the department four glass stems. They were cracked before we even turned the key. - T.B.

Ingredients
Dry stocks remaining in tin-lined bins: bulk cacao, refined sugar, whole almonds, dried spices, powdered milk, roasted coffee beans.

Perishables - including fresh butter, cream, open fruit syrups, and fresh fruit pulps - distributed to staff households and the parish kitchen on Calle Estados Unidos to prevent spoilage.

Twenty-three sample jars on the upper shelf remain unidentified. Gummed labels washed off during the storeroom roof leak in May and replacement ink ran.

Handwritten beside entry: Smell everything before you put a spoon in it. This means you, Felix, if these boxes ever get forwarded to South Africa. Half of those jars are raw bittering trials. - T.B.

Recipe Records
Approved production formulas have been duplicated in duplicate cipher and forwarded to San Francisco via diplomatic post. Working laboratory logs will remain locked in the station vault until freight space is secure.

Working notebooks must remain intact. Do not tear out discarded pages, crossed-out measurements, or tasting critiques. An unrecorded failure simply guarantees someone else will waste fifty pounds of good cacao making the exact same mistake three years from now.

Handwritten beneath paragraph: Yes, leave the apricot-cardamom batch in the ledger. It tasted like perfumed turpentine, but we need the record so Chas doesn't attempt to put it in a bar. - Teddy

Outstanding Work
Trial 221 - toasted rice infusion: clean flavor, but the oil separates from the butter after four days on the shelf.
Trial 228 - coffee-chocolate emulsion: grain forms along the cooling curve below 16°C. Do not schedule for production.
Trial 231 - lime cream filling: sharp, clean citrus profile, but curdles fresh dairy solids inside forty-eight hours.
Trial 236 - black tea and sweet orange peel: hold formula for postwar trial.
Trial 240 - dark cane syrup sample sent from Tangier via Lisbon packet: heavy sulfur, overly dense. Failed in test ganache.

Handwritten beside Trial 240: Zach swears Moroccan bakers use it for tea breads. They are welcome to keep it. - T.B.

Final Note
This suspension is an operational pause, not a liquidation. No machinery is to be sold, no fixtures removed, and no formulation records discarded without formal Board resolution from San Francisco.

When international sea routes reopen and regular ingredient commerce resumes, recipe development can be re-established wherever plant capacity, ingredients, and staff can be assembled under proper supervision.

Handwritten at bottom of page:
Tied down the tarps and locked the street door at 6:40. The power was cut for the evening, so had to finish by lantern. Hard to look at the benches without a kettle humming.

Kept the safe key and my working book.
We'll set these pans up again somewhere.
- Teddy Baumeister

Teddy Baumeister's Reykjavík Notebook
Working notes kept during the establishment of the Secret Test Kitchen, 1946.

12 February 1946 - San Francisco
Spent most of the afternoon arguing with the Board about Iceland.

Uncle Felix looked at the map for perhaps ten seconds and asked whether I was aware that cacao doesn't grow anywhere near the Arctic Circle. Yes, Felix. I am aware.

That is rather the point.

Buenos Aires was excellent when we needed a proper laboratory attached to the South American trade. It was also known to every supplier, freight broker, commercial representative, and confectionery salesman who ever did business with us. If we're setting up experimental work again after the war, I don't want the next Schokolade Weltreich fellow renting an office across the street and counting our ingredient crates.

Reykjavík is small, isolated, and sitting in the middle of the North Atlantic. It has a working commercial harbor, an airfield the British spent half the war building, and more communications infrastructure than a city of its size has any reasonable business possessing. We don't need shiploads of cacao for recipe trials. We need fifty pounds here, a sack there, six jars of something peculiar from Tangier, and a way to get the finished formula back to the factories.

The climate helps too. Half the expense of keeping a chocolate laboratory behaved in Buenos Aires was fighting the summer heat. Reykjavík seems perfectly willing to refrigerate the entire country for us at no charge.

Then there is the hot water. Pipes carrying geothermal water straight into buildings. No coal furnace, no oil delivery every week, no praying that somebody remembered to order fuel before the ship sailed. After 1942, that alone is enough to make me sentimental.

Joseph still thinks I'm mad.

Alex said, "If you can make the numbers work, go and look at it."

Good enough for me.

3 April 1946 - Reykjavík
Arrived yesterday in rain blowing almost sideways across the harbor. This morning was bright sunshine. By lunch it was sleeting. Nobody here considers any of this remarkable.

Reykjavík is not quite the sleepy fishing town I had imagined. The war seems to have picked the place up by the shoulders and shaken it. Trucks everywhere, corrugated iron houses going up wherever anyone can find room, old military sheds mixed among new workshops, foreign machinery sitting on the quays, and people pouring into town from the countryside faster than housing can be built for them.

I was offered two former military barracks as possible premises and refused both. Families are living in these things. Some have two households partitioned into buildings that were never intended to house one comfortably. Baumeister Confections can afford not to throw somebody out of a roof just so I can have a tasting room.

Third property was much better: an old military stores and maintenance building near Öskjuhlíð, ugly as sin, concrete floor, thick walls, loading doors at the rear, proper drainage, and far enough from the commercial center that nobody has any reason to visit unless invited. One end was used for vehicle parts, judging by the oil soaked into the floor. The other still has a British inventory number painted above the door.

I love it.

19 April 1946
The plumber opened a valve this morning and hot water from the earth started running through our radiators.

I stood there grinning at a pipe for an embarrassing length of time.

The locals are unsurprised. Apparently Reykjavík has been extending these hot-water lines for years, and the utility is being reorganized again now. To me, after watching Buenos Aires fight for every ton of coal in 1942, it feels like witchcraft. There is a faint mineral smell when the system first runs, but the heat is steady and doesn't require a boiler room eating imported fuel all winter.

We've divided the old stores building into three zones. Warm preparation room at one end, main formulation benches in the center, and a cooler room against the north wall for setting, storage, and anything likely to misbehave above sixty-five degrees Fahrenheit. The outside air can do most of that work for free.

The electricians are less pleased with me. I asked for separate circuits on every heated vessel, the grinders, refrigeration cabinet, laboratory lamps, and ventilation fans. One of them stared at my diagram and asked - in very good English - whether I was planning to manufacture chocolate or launch a battleship.

Fair question.

6 May 1946
Started Icelandic lessons properly today.

Nearly everyone I deal with has at least some English after six years of British and American soldiers coming through here, which makes it very easy for a foreigner to become lazy. I don't intend to live in somebody else's country and make the grocer translate "cream" for me every time I walk through the door.

Today's useful vocabulary:
súkkulaði - chocolate
kaffi - coffee
sykur - sugar
rjómi - cream
smjör - butter
mjólk - milk

Góðan daginn. Good day.
Takk fyrir. Thank you.
Ég heiti Teddy. My name is Teddy.
Ég er að læra íslensku. I am learning Icelandic.

That last sentence has already become necessary because the moment I attempt the first three, people assume I know far more Icelandic than I actually do and answer at full speed.

I am also learning that surnames do not behave the way an American expects. Calling everybody "Mr. Jónsson" makes me sound ridiculous because half the country seems to be somebody's son or daughter and everyone simply uses first names. I spent three days assuming a clerk and her father had different family names before somebody finally explained patronymics to me over coffee.

The letters are getting me too. Þ is not a P. Ð is not a D. I wrote rjómi correctly on my shopping list and then pronounced it so badly the dairy woman reached for rye flour.

We'll get there.

28 May 1946
I'm beginning to understand why people become attached to this place.

The harbor wakes up before I do. Fishing boats coming in, gulls screaming over the roofs, carts and lorries moving boxes before breakfast. Lunch is usually fish unless somebody has gone to considerable effort to make it something else. I've developed a taste for skyr, although I still cannot decide whether it belongs at breakfast, dessert, or beside a laboratory balance while I'm too busy to eat properly. Apparently the answer is all three.

Dark rye bread with butter is dangerous. I have eaten half a loaf today without noticing.

The city still has American habits clinging to it from the occupation. You hear English expressions mixed into conversations, imported records playing in cafés, and young people who can tell you the difference between three American automobile makes while their grandparents regard the whole business with suspicion. Then somebody corrects my Icelandic because I used an English word where a perfectly good Icelandic one exists. There is a stubbornness about the language I rather admire.

The strangest adjustment is the light. It is nearly June and night has apparently been cancelled. I went to bed at eleven last night, looked through the curtains, decided it could not possibly be eleven, checked my watch, checked the clock in the kitchen, and finally accepted that Iceland does not care what my body thinks nighttime should look like.

Bought heavier curtains this afternoon.

14 June 1946
First crates from Buenos Aires opened today.

Not everything survived storage. Two copper pans have green spotting where somebody missed a patch of moisture before wrapping them, and one grinder has seized completely. The balance is fine. Formula books are dry. Trial logs intact.

Found the old apricot-cardamom page.

Still dreadful.

I also found the safe key in the pocket where I put it four years ago, which is somehow more satisfying than it ought to be.

We've reused what we could and bought the rest locally. The benches are Icelandic timber over steel frames. A machinist in town fabricated new grinder collars from my Buenos Aires drawings and improved the adjustment thread without being asked. I complained for perhaps thirty seconds before admitting his version was better.

The laboratory finally sounds right again. Belts, grinder teeth, water moving through the pipes, somebody banging a tray against a bench in the next room. I hadn't realized how much I'd missed ordinary laboratory noise until it came back.

Felix has started calling the place the "Secret Test Kitchen." I told him it sounds like something children would build behind a hedge. He has now used the name in three Board telegrams, so I suppose I've lost that battle.

2 July 1946
Everything is finally in working order.

No sign outside except the street number. Ingredient parcels come through the ordinary freight office and arrive in quantities too small to interest anyone on the docks. The formulation books stay in the safe unless we're actively using them, and finished recipes leave Reykjavík as copies rather than originals. Production can happen in Zürich, San Francisco, Tokyo, Wellington, wherever the Board wants it. Nobody needs to know where the first six experimental batches were made.

That is why Iceland works. We are not trying to manufacture a million chocolate bars here. We are trying to make one recipe correctly, break it, fix it, make it again, and send the answer somewhere else.

Alex wired this morning. Apparently the new Chocolatier is progressing faster than expected and the Board intends to send them north once they have enough original work to justify using the laboratory.

Good. I have spent four months building this place and arguing with electricians, freight agents, customs clerks, plumbers, carpenters, and the Icelandic language itself.

It will be nice to finally argue about chocolate again.

My dear Sean,

Well. Australia again.

I had forgotten how quiet this country gets the moment you leave the coast behind. The passenger train only ran as far as the railhead, and after that it was two days in the back of an old Dodge truck with a cracked manifold that smelled like burning oil every time we hit a sand ridge. I have red dirt in my stockings, in the lining of my coat, and somehow inside the seal of my travel inkwell. It’s the kind of fine dust that never quite washes out; you just have to decide to live with it.

I found someone out here, Sean.

I’m writing that down carefully so I don't let my hands run away with me. He didn’t know you personally. He was based at the same airfield complex in England toward the end of '44, running maintenance and transport. A man named McInnes - leather-skinned, missing half an ear from a tractor accident, and about as conversational as a fence post. I had to drag every sentence out of him with pliers.

I asked him straight out about your squadron. He stood there leaning against a post, looked at my shoes, spat into the dust, and told me, "Officially? He went down with the kite. Most of 'em did."

I told him I hadn't crossed two oceans and three hundred miles of desert track to have an official casualty telegram read back to me by an Australian.

That made him look up. He squinted at me for a long time, rubbed his chin, and finally grunted that there had been a hell of an argument in the operations hut after that mission. One of the pilots from your flight came back shouting at the debriefing officer because he swore he’d seen a canopy open below your B-24 as she went into the soup. Not wing fabric tearing off. A chute. Full and white, dropping through the clouds.

I asked who saw it. He took half a minute to remember, staring off toward the red rock like the answer was written on the sandstone.

"Hardy," he told me. "Tom Hardy. Captain, I think. Flew the right wing. Stubborn bastard, wouldn't let the room move on."

Sean, my knees went completely weak. I had to grab the side of the truck just to keep my feet under me.

A name. A real name, from a man who was actually in the room, not another clerk in Washington telling me a file was closed.

I asked what became of Hardy’s report. McInnes got shifty then. He wouldn't look at me. He muttered that there was a liaison officer attached to the group - a German defector working under Allied intelligence who sat in on the aircrew debriefings. The German told Hardy he was exhausted, that the flak had rattled his nerves, and that he was imagining things to make himself feel better about losing his lead ship. The statement never made it into the official squadron log. McInnes said nobody wanted to start an inquiry with the war ending and half the group packing their kits for home.

I wanted to hit him. I really did. You would have laughed your head off seeing me standing in the red dust with my fists clenched, glaring at a cattleman twice my size.

He gave me three names before I left. Rick is already pulling service records in San Francisco, trying to find where Thomas Hardy went after the surrender. If Hardy is back in the States, or back in England, or anywhere on this earth, I am going to find him and hear every single second of that debriefing from his own mouth.

I'm trying to be sensible. I can hear your voice in my ear telling me not to run off half-cocked. A parachute doesn't tell me where you landed. It doesn't explain why your name was never on a Stalag roster, or why you weren't on the repatriation trains when the camps opened in May. Maybe Hardy was mistaken. Maybe the clouds were thick and he saw a flare chute or an engine cowling and his mind played a trick on him.

Maybe. But for two years, all I’ve had was an empty telegram from the War Department. Now I have a pilot who saw white silk.

Margaret asked me in Zürich before I boarded the boat if I had found anything real yet. She tries to sound so grown up now, Sean - she’s nineteen and trying to carry the house so I don't have to. I lied to her. I told her I was just following up on shipping routes for the Board. Thomas knew I was lying, but he didn't press it; he has your habit of going quiet when he’s worried. And Cora... Cora still asks if you’re coming home on the next steamer every time the post arrives. I couldn't bear handing them a rumor and watching their faces when it didn't pan out.

So I'm keeping it right here on this paper.

Someone saw you get out, Sean.

I'm leaving for the railhead at sunrise. Then Sydney, then the packet boat back to Europe. And then I’m going to find this Tom Hardy, and whoever that German liaison officer was.

All my love,
Alex

Morocco Fine Coffees
Special Orders Desk Book - Zachariah Tangye
Selected working pages from the Tangier shop.

How the Desk Works
The ordinary shop trade pays the rent. Special Orders are where the interesting money is.

A hotel, club, shipping company, railway dining room, embassy household, merchant family, or private buyer asks for something in a quantity large enough that the usual retail counter cannot sensibly handle it. We agree on the product, quantity, delivery point, deadline, and price. If the order is suitable for one of our partner manufacturers, I offer it onward and retain the brokerage percentage agreed in the partnership ledger.

Never promise stock before confirming that somebody can actually make it. A customer who hears "yes" on Monday and "sorry" on Thursday remembers Thursday.

Likewise, never reject an odd request simply because it sounds odd. Wealthy people become remarkably specific when they are spending someone else's entertainment budget.

Margin note: This includes bankers. Especially bankers.

Telegram Procedure
If the manufacturer is in Tangier, speak to them. Telegrams cost money and half the meaning disappears when every unnecessary word is charged by the wire office.

If they have already left port, send only what is required to decide whether the order is worth accepting:

1. Client or delivery city.
2. Product requested.
3. Number of cases.
4. Price offered.
5. Latest acceptable delivery date.
6. Any condition likely to make a sensible person refuse it.
