Do not waste twelve paid words telling someone an order is "extremely exciting." If the money is good, the figures will accomplish that on their own.

Our partners travel constantly, so replies may come through another Baumeister shop, a hotel desk, railway telegraph office, shipping agent, or whichever commercial address they left with us last. Keep the movement card current. Sending a profitable order to Zürich while the recipient is already halfway to Havana is an excellent way to turn profit into stationery.

Example Wires

TANGIER 14 MAY
URGENT ORDER CASABLANCA MERCHANTS CLUB FORTY CASES MILK CHOCOLATE SQUARES DELIVERY BEFORE TWENTY SECOND STOP OFFER 18,000 DOLLARS STOP ADVISE ACCEPTANCE TODAY - ZACH

Good order. Straightforward goods, short sea or rail movement, respectable buyer. Accept unless production is already committed elsewhere.

TANGIER 3 JUNE
PRIVATE CLIENT MARSEILLE REQUESTS SIXTY CASES COFFEE PRODUCT WITH VANILLA STOP WILL PAY 31,500 DOLLARS IF DELIVERED TEN DAYS STOP CLIENT INSISTS FRESH STOCK STOP REPLY YES OR NO - ZACH

Fresh stock matters here. Do not manufacture three weeks early merely because the factory is idle.

TANGIER 19 JUNE
HOTEL BUYER CAIRO REQUESTS NINETY CASES ASSORTED TRUFFLES STOP EXCELLENT PRICE BUT DELIVERY WINDOW SIX DAYS STOP DO NOT ACCEPT UNLESS STOCK OR FACTORY CAPACITY ALREADY AVAILABLE - ZACH

This is exactly why the deadline goes in the telegram. Ninety cases at a beautiful price become ninety cases of trouble if the ship leaves on Tuesday.

Client Book
Keep notes after every delivery. Who paid promptly? Who complained? Who ordered again? Who tried to change the quantity after the goods were already packed? A good client list is not a collection of names; it is a record of behavior.

I mark reliable repeat customers with a blue pencil. Slow payers get red. Anybody who disputes an agreed price after accepting delivery gets a black line through the page and can buy their chocolate somewhere else.

Margin note: Salma says the black line is theatrical. She is correct. I intend to continue doing it.

The most valuable contacts are not always the largest buyers. Hotel concierges hear about weddings before confectioners do. Shipping agents know when a passenger liner needs provisions. Bank clerks know when an office is planning a reception. Coffee merchants hear complaints about bad desserts. One useful introduction can produce six orders over the next year.

That is the part Father never quite understood. He thinks in accounts already on the books. I prefer the ones that have not reached us yet.

Partnerships
A shop partner receives better wholesale terms because I want their goods moving through my door. In return, I can put their factories in front of buyers they would never meet on their own.

The arrangement only works if both sides answer quickly and keep their word. When I wire an order, I need an acceptance or refusal before the customer loses patience. When the manufacturer promises seventy-five cases, I need seventy-five cases. Not sixty-eight and an explanation.

The first few partnerships were expensive to establish. Telegraph charges, clerical time, deposit guarantees, new account books, credit checks, sample shipments, and a truly absurd amount of correspondence all had to be paid before a single order came back through the system.

Worth it.

Once the network is moving, one shop can hear about an order in Tangier, wire a manufacturer in another country, arrange delivery to a third, collect payment through a fourth, and have the whole transaction entered into the books before the people involved ever meet each other.

Grandfather Jarrah would have understood it immediately.

Current Note - 1946
Alex has sent another operator my way. Says they are rebuilding the factories and need proper retail partners rather than simply unloading cases wherever somebody will take them.

Good.

If they can manufacture reliably, answer a telegram before the client dies of old age, and resist the urge to accept every ridiculous deadline dangled in front of them, I can make this useful very quickly.

I will need capital to reopen several dormant accounts and get the regular cable traffic moving again. I can cover most of it from the shop, but if our new partner wants access to the network, they can put something on the table too.

- Zachariah Tangye

AIRCREW DEBRIEFING - INTERNAL LIAISON MEMORANDUM
Recovered copy. Author: W. Fleischer, Liaison Section. Late 1944.

RE: FLETCHER, Sean - B-24 aircraft missing following combat operations
WITNESS: HARDY, Thomas - Captain, pilot

Capt. Hardy was interviewed following return of the formation and has repeated an observation concerning the loss of Fletcher's aircraft. He states that after the damaged bomber dropped below formation and entered cloud, he observed what appeared to be one fully deployed white parachute beneath the aircraft.

Hardy estimates that the sighting lasted only several seconds. Exact altitude and distance could not be supplied. Visibility at the time was poor owing to cloud, smoke, evasive maneuvering and continuing anti-aircraft fire. No second crewman has independently confirmed the observation.

Capt. Hardy remains unusually certain of what he saw and became argumentative when the limitations of the sighting were explained to him. He insists the object was a parachute and rejects the possibility of detached aircraft fabric, flare equipment or debris.

In my judgment, the statement should not be treated as sufficient grounds to amend the existing missing-aircraft report. Aircrew returning from heavy combat frequently misjudge distance, shape and movement, particularly where a close associate has been lost. Hardy's conviction is therefore not, by itself, evidence of accuracy.

No useful purpose would be served by circulating the statement beyond the present intelligence file unless corroborating evidence becomes available. The operational report should continue to record Fletcher and crew as missing with aircraft.

The separate witness sheet prepared by Capt. Hardy is not required for higher review. Retain with local debriefing material.

W. FLEISCHER
Liaison Section

Handwritten notation beneath signature:
Hardy returned again at 0730 asking whether the statement had gone forward. Advised matter was closed. He was dissatisfied but departed without further incident.

My dear Sean,

It is nearly one in the morning, and I am writing this with the tall windows thrown wide open because the room refuses to cool down and somebody downstairs has decided that midnight is an ideal hour to start dragging furniture across the tile floor. I can hear car horns down in the plaza, the occasional harbor train whistle drifting in from the coast, and Rick finally gave up and went to bed after spending twenty minutes reminding me that Callao will still be sitting on the Pacific in the morning. Yes, thank you, Rick. I am reasonably aware of geography.

Hardy’s statement is spread out across the desk beside me. The paper keeps curling up in this coastal damp, so I have the hotel ashtray holding down one corner and the heavy water pitcher anchoring the Callao notes. Father would have an absolute stroke if he saw my filing system, but it works.

Hardy saw you, Sean. I have written that down on scrap paper half a dozen times tonight, and every time I look at it, it knocks the breath clean out of me. He didn’t report a vague flash of canvas or some piece of falling wreckage; he was so specific about seeing your canopy open that he ended up shouting at the debriefing officer for trying to soften his words. McInnes remembered the entire row because Hardy simply refused to back down: "No, sir, I saw the chute. I saw the full white canopy open and drop into the overcast." That sounds like someone you would have shared a drink with. In fact, from what McInnes told me, you two were thick as thieves.

It is typical of my luck that while I was scouring Australia for the man who saw you get out alive, the Army had already reassigned Hardy to Tokyo with the occupation forces. But his original statement stayed behind in the squadron records, and underneath the typed summary, he took a pen and added in his own hand: "I want it noted again that the chute was fully deployed. It was a canopy, not a piece of the wing." I sat there in the archives staring at that line until Rick asked if I was feeling faint. I told him I was fine, and then immediately started crying into my handkerchief, which was terribly convincing.

And then we went to Geneva.

Sean, your name is in the International Red Cross intake register. Not on a missing casualty list, and not as an unconfirmed rumor passed along by a returning airman. An actual German camp clerk sat at a desk in late 1944 and entered your name into the book: Fletcher, Sean P. Captain. American aircrew. Prisoner.

You were alive. You survived the jump, someone picked you up, and you were standing in front of a desk answering intake questions. I keep thinking about how mundane and ordinary that piece of paper is. When the clerk in Geneva pointed to the line, I blurted out, "That's my husband," as if she hadn't just spent two days watching me pace her reading room. She was very gentle about it, but Rick still had to make duplicate photostats before she would let me hold the original again because my hands were trembling so badly.

The maddening part - the thing that has kept me awake for three nights straight - is that the record simply stops there. There is no transfer log to a permanent Stalag, no medical sheet, and no repatriation manifest when the camps were opened in the spring. You enter the ledger, and then you evaporate into thin air. When I asked the archivist if entire prisoners routinely go missing between folders, she didn't have an answer.

That brings me to Fleischer.

I finally read his confidential memorandum regarding Hardy’s debriefing. There is a single sentence in that file that makes my blood boil every time I look at it: "No useful purpose would be served by circulating this observation." Hardy watches my husband bail out of a burning Liberator, and this German liaison officer decides it serves no useful purpose to inform his family or the squadron. Rick had to physically take the paper away from me because I was gripping the margin so hard the corner began to tear. He told me it was evidence; I told him I’d like to feed it to Fleischer with a spoon. Rick sighed and told me not to put threats in writing, so naturally I am putting it right here in my letter to you.

That memo is why we started digging into Fleischer’s personal communications instead of just the military files. Rick found references to an old commercial forwarding account tucked into correspondence between Lisbon and South America. That is why we boarded the steamer for Peru, and that is why we spent this morning down in the harbor at Callao.

Callao is loud, filthy, and smells intensely of salt brine, diesel exhaust, and wet cattle hides sitting in the sun. The forwarding agency sits three flights up over a ship chandler, with a staircase so rotted the handrail wobbles if you breathe on it. The office itself has two ceiling fans that do nothing but stir the flies around, and a manager who told us with great dignity that their wartime client records were strictly confidential and that he had never heard of our reference number.

I set an envelope of Swiss francs on his desk blotter. Suddenly his memory improved remarkably. I know, I know - you are giving me that wry look of yours from across the room. But it worked.

The account exists: F-17.

It has been running since late '44. It is an account tied to Schokolade Weltreich, but there is not a single shipment of cocoa butter, sugar, vanilla, or machinery parts attached to it. It is entirely cable fees, forwarding drafts, and explicit instructions to reroute correspondence away from San Francisco, away from Zürich, and away from military casualty bureaus. The old clerk with the heavy spectacles remembered it clearly. He told me it was a very strange account - always instructions on where letters must not go, and always authorized by the same initials: W.F.

Wolf Fleischer.

The clerk let me copy the ledger entries on their ancient Remington typewriter while he hovered over my shoulder complaining that I was hitting the keys hard enough to break the carriage. There is a payment notation from early last year showing funds forwarded through an intermediary in the Caribbean, followed by another draft where the destination line was left blank.

I have to be careful here. I can hear you telling me not to build an entire case out of three letters and an invoice. A routing account in South America doesn't mean you were brought through Peru, and it doesn't mean Fleischer is keeping you in a warehouse down the street. For all I know, he was using company funds to wash his own dirty money through neutral ports before the Reich collapsed.

But Sean, the pattern is too deliberate. Fleischer buries Hardy’s eyewitness statement in England. Your prisoner trail vanishes in Germany. And then Fleischer’s private account starts moving money through the Americas to keep mail from reaching the people looking for you. I am not walking away from that thread.

Tomorrow morning, Rick and I are heading back down to the docks. The clerk thinks there may be duplicate cable manifests in the maritime customs house if we can persuade the harbormaster to pull the old boxes down from the rafters. Persuasion takes a little cash down here, but I have another envelope ready in my purse.

Margaret sent a letter from Zürich that arrived yesterday. She claims the house is running smoothly and that I shouldn't worry about anything at home, which is her polite way of saying the plumbing in the scullery has started leaking again. She sounds more like you every month. Thomas has been sitting at the kitchen table with a calendar and my copy of the Geneva register, trying to calculate the days between your intake and the end of the war; he hid the notebook under his sweater when Margaret walked into the room. He worries in complete silence just like his father, and it breaks my heart. And Cora wants to know if there are llamas walking down the streets in Lima. I wrote back on hotel stationery to tell her I haven't seen one yet, but I'm keeping an eye out.

I miss you.

I’ve spent months in drafty offices and train compartments trying to keep from falling apart, but tonight is different. I am not sitting in this hotel room trying to talk myself into believing you survived. You got out of that plane, Sean. You were on the ground, and someone made a deliberate effort to make sure I never found out where you went.

Fine. Then I'll find Fleischer, and I'll find where he sent you.

As always, please keep holding on, my love. I am on the trail now.

All my love,
Alex

UNITED STATES ARMY AIR FORCES
EIGHTH AIR FORCE - AIRCREW DEBRIEFING STATEMENT

WITNESS: Capt. Thomas Hardy, Pilot
SUBJECT: Loss of B-24 aircraft piloted by Capt. Sean P. Fletcher
DATE: Late 1944
AREA OF OPERATION: Central Germany

STATEMENT:

I was flying on the right side of Capt. Fletcher's aircraft during withdrawal from the target area. The formation was under heavy anti-aircraft fire at the time.

I saw at least one flak burst strike or detonate very close to the left wing and inboard engine section of Fletcher's aircraft. Almost immediately afterward the aircraft began losing speed and altitude and fell out of formation to the left.

There was heavy smoke from the aircraft. I could not determine whether the left wing itself had failed, but the aircraft was no longer maintaining formation and was descending rapidly toward a heavy layer of cloud below us.

Before Fletcher's aircraft disappeared into the cloud I observed one white parachute below and slightly behind it.

The canopy was fully open.

I had the parachute in sight for several seconds. I could not identify the person beneath it and cannot state the exact altitude at which the jump was made. I did not observe any additional parachutes before losing visual contact with the aircraft.

I am certain that what I saw was a parachute and not detached fabric from the aircraft. The canopy had the regular rounded shape of an opened personnel parachute and descended separately from the aircraft wreckage.

Because the formation remained under fire and continued away from the area, I was unable to circle or make any further observation of the ground below. The damaged aircraft subsequently disappeared from my view in cloud and smoke.

I therefore believe that at least one member of Capt. Fletcher's crew successfully left the aircraft before it was lost.

I have given the above statement to the best of my recollection and have read it before signing.

Thomas Hardy
Captain, Air Corps

Handwritten beneath signature:
I want it noted again that the chute was open. I saw the full canopy, not a piece of the wing. - T.H.
Prisoner Record: Capt. Sean P. Fletcher, 1944

PRIVATE DISBURSEMENTS / FORWARDING REGISTER

Purpose: Handling, storage and onward correspondence

Same file reference Alexandra Fletcher traced in Peru. Fleischer was still using it seven months after the war ended in Europe. - K.C.

Whatever Fleischer was moving, it did not stop when the lorry did. - K.C.

Not even pretending this was company business by this point. - K.C.

Three lines have been underlined heavily in pencil beside this entry.

Handwritten below:
The paper trail stops here. Succotz sits on the Mopan, directly opposite Xunantunich. Fleischer either stopped caring about receipts after this point, or he specifically did not want the route written down.

There is one person I know who can make sense of what lies west of this.

Cambria Equivel - Xunantunich.

If Fletcher went beyond Succotz, ask her before asking anyone else. Do not send through the Schokolade Weltreich cable office. - K.C.

Loose Sheet Found with Register
Alexandra,

I copied nothing because I could not safely leave the originals behind.

Fleischer buried these payments among ordinary forwarding costs. That is why nobody noticed them. A warehouse fee here, a road contractor there, a few hundred dollars for provisions, then another account on the next page. We process hundreds of charges like these every month. Unless somebody already knows which reference to follow, it looks like nothing.

The Callao number is the same one you showed me. From there I followed the account forward until it reached British Honduras.

I cannot tell you that Sean Fletcher is at the end of this route. I won't insult you by pretending these papers prove something they don't.

What I can tell you is that Fleischer was paying to move somebody or something inland from Belize, that the account continued west through El Cayo and Benque Viejo, and that his recorded expenses stopped at Succotz. After that, he used cash.

Cambria Equivel works out of Xunantunich and knows the western tracks, river crossings and settlements better than anyone I have dealt with in that district. If there is another end to this trail, she has the best chance of finding it.

One other thing: don't come looking for me through company channels. Fleischer is not stupid. By the time he notices these sheets are missing, I intend to be somewhere he isn't.

- Katherine
Letter: Thomas Hardy to Sean Fletcher

Fletcher, you old son of a gun.

I'm sitting at a desk in Tokyo right now, and I still can't quite believe I'm writing this. The chocolatier who's delivering this just gave me the news, and I nearly knocked over my coffee. You're alive.

I knew it. I knew it the day your B-24 took that flak. I saw your silk open before you hit the tree line, clear as day. I filed the report the second my boots hit the tarmac, but that snake of a liaison officer, Fleischer, buried it. He told the brass it was just combat stress and shut me down. I spent the last year half-thinking I was losing my mind, but I never stopped believing you made it out.

Then again, if you could walk away laughing from that busted landing gear incident back in '43, I figured no jungle in the world could keep you down forever.

I hear you're finally back in Switzerland with Alex. Give her my absolute best. I remember how her letters - and those care packages of Baumeister chocolates - were the only things that kept you going on the airstrip. It sounds like she fought just as hard to find you as you did to survive.

We missed you in the 8th, buddy. Take all the time you need to heal up. When you're ready, the first round is on me.

Your wingman,
Tom Hardy
